newsitem.title: FRANCE: Doors set to open at France's Mitterrand library.
newsitem.headline: Doors set to open at France's Mitterrand library.

text.p: France's mammoth new Francois Mitterrand national library, a costly steel and glass complex by the banks of the Seine, prepared to open its doors on Tuesday as the final memorial to the book-loving late president.

But President Jacques Chirac planned to keep a low profile at Tuesday's opening ceremonies for the building, a project launched by his Socialist predecessor which he fought against while mayor of Paris.

The conservative Chirac, a devotee of Japanese art who shows little public interest in books, planned no speech at the ceremony opening the Left Bank landmark named after Mitterrand, an author and avowed lover of literature, aides said.
"The president will make a tour of the library's rooms. There will be no speech, no ribbon cutting," a Chirac aide said.
Chirac, who served as Paris mayor before being elected president in May 1995, tried to block or delay construction of the complex during the early 1990s, library officials said.

Mitterrand, who left office in May 1995 and died last January, acknowledged during one of his last interviews as president that he had rushed construction so the complex would be too far along to be torn down when voters threw out France's Socialist government in 1993 general elections.

The library, designed by architect Dominique Perrault, consists of four L-shaped glass towers, each 18 stories high, surrounding a sunken urban forest of wild pines, elms and birches. There are also six levels buried underground.
Officials said the project cost some eight billion francs ($1.5 billion), well above initial projections

It is the last in a series of expensive and controversial Mitterrand public works projects that altered the landscape of the French capital, including the controversial glass pyramid entrance to the Louvre museum, sprawling science and music "cities" and a vast new home for the Finance Ministry.

Advance publicity for the new library has centred on its high-tech computer system, elegant furnishings and sumptuous interior design, contrasting bold woodwork with huge steel-girded windows, reinforced concrete walls and deep orange-red carpeting.
Only one level of the building will initially be open to the general public, beginning on Friday. A second level will eventually be opened, but to scholars only.
The existing national library's main collection of 10 million volumes will not be moved into the new complex until 1998 and even then will be kept in rooms accessible only to library workers.
The books will be transferred from the current national library in the capital's second district at an average rate of 25,000 to 30,000 volumes a day over the next two years.

The old national library, located between the Rue de Richelieu and the Rue Vivienne to the north of the Palais Royal, will be renamed after Cardinal de Richelieu, who served as chief minister to King Louis XIII from 1624 until his death in 1642.
It will become France's main depository for the state's collections of manuscripts, engravings, maps, music, coins and theatrical items.
